newsitem.title: THAILAND: YEARENDER - Thai insurance growth seen slowing.
newsitem.headline: YEARENDER - Thai insurance growth seen slowing.

text.p: Growth in Thailand's insurance industry is expected to ease next year with higher damage claims anticipated, industry sources said.

"The insurance industry will grow at a slower pace than this year in line with the overall slowing of the economy," Saravoot Phasuvanichphongse, the president of the General Insurance Association, told Reuters.
"The slowing economy next year will also result in higher risk and damage claims from fire and car accidents by the insured," Saravoot said.
The central Bank of Thailand has projected that the Thai gross domestic product will expand 7.1 percent in 1997 from about 6.7 percent in 1996 and 8.7 percent in 1995.

"The insurance industry normally rises twice as much as the gross domestic product growth. The slow economic growth will begin to have an apparent impact on the industry next year," said Surachai Sirivallop, president of Thai Reinsurance Plc.
Saravoot said insurance premiums are expected to grow about 10 percent a year in 1996 and 1997, after more than 30 percent annual growth in the past few years.

Thai Reinsurance's Surachai said the total of insurance premiums in the industry was expected to rise to 71 billion baht ($2.84 billion) in 1997 from 62 billion baht in 1996 and 53 billion baht in 1995.
Premiums on car insurance account for the largest portion with annual premiums totalling about 40 billion baht currently, according to the insurance association's data.
"The slow economy will significantly affect car sales. The number of cars sold will continue to decline next year," Surachai said.
The association expects the premiums on car insurance to rise 13 percent next year, after increases of 16-17 percent in 1996 and 20 percent in 1995.
Government plans to issue more new insurance licences will have a significant impact on existing insurance companies as the market was already crowded, the association's Saravoot said.
"There are currently 62 insurance companies, while the existing volume is very thin. If the government granted many more licences, it will substantially affect existing companies," he said.
